📌 Zcash sets July 28 hard fork to seal Orchard after critical bug 

⚠️ Zcash founder Zooko Wilcox has explained how the network’s July 28 Ironwood hard fork will address uncertainty around a critical flaw in the Orchard shielded pool. The upgrade will not identify or freeze individual counterfeit coins. Instead, it will seal the old pool and limit how much ZEC can leave. 

🔖 Ironwood, also known as NU6.3, is scheduled to activate at block 3,428,143 on July 28. The upgrade will retire the current Orchard pool and introduce a new shielded pool based on the corrected circuit. According to Zcash’s official Ironwood user update, users will no longer be able to send or receive ZEC inside the old Orchard pool after activation. Funds can leave only through the turnstile, which prevents more ZEC from exiting than legitimately entered.

⭐️ The Zcash team said it believes the flaw was “unlikely to have been exploited,” but users cannot independently prove no counterfeit ZEC was created. Ironwood aims to trap any excess value inside the old pool rather than allow it to enter wider circulation. Security researcher Taylor Hornby discovered the Orchard flaw on May 29 while auditing the shielded system. The bug could have allowed an attacker to create counterfeit ZEC inside Orchard without leaving an obvious public record.

Two weeks into the latest round of fighting, the US and Iran are trading calibrated strikes while Trump talks about a “massive attack” big enough to force a peace deal.

CENTCOM has now logged 13 consecutive nights of strikes on Iranian military targets around the Strait of Hormuz, officially to “degrade” Iran’s ability to threaten commercial shipping. 

Iran answers by hitting US bases and allied facilities in Kuwait and Bahrain, and by having the Revolutionary Guard declare Hormuz “closed” while tankers creep through under escort. 

In parallel, Yemen’s Houthi militants — Iran’s Axis of Resistance franchise — claim drone and missile strikes on Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and announce a blockade on Saudi shipping through Bab el‑Mandeb, turning a second narrow channel into a risk point.

Trump tells Axios he’s “close to making a decision” on attacks “bigger than ever before,” says Iran “hasn’t received enough pain yet,” and posts on Truth Social that any damage to ships or cargo “will be paid for by Iranian money” frozen under US control. 

The US holds about $2 billion in blocked Iranian funds at home and much larger sums abroad; Iran’s foreign minister calls the idea of using those assets to pay for future claims “an incendiary precedent.” 

At the same time, Trump threatens to destroy “one bridge or power plant” every time Iran hits shipping, while Tehran warns that if he does, it will escalate against regional energy infrastructure.

The result is a war that the White House insists is limited while it quietly pushes every maritime chokepoint closer to crisis. Hormuz, which used to carry about a fifth of global energy flows, has slowed to a trickle. 

Bab el‑Mandeb is now partially avoided after the Houthi blockade announcement, even as Chinese‑owned tankers test the route under risk. 

Oil sits above $100, gas above $4, and Trump — who last month cited the risk of a global economic crash as a reason to accept a truce — is back to promising “major military punishment” against Iran and the Houthis if they touch commercial ships.

The oddest part is the rhetoric: “peace deal” via threats to blow up bridges and power plants, “security of shipping” via nightly airstrikes, “compensation” via raiding frozen assets.
